pedagogy.summary: A linear function y = mx + c produces a straight-line graph, where m (the gradient) is the constant rate of change — the line's steepness and direction — and c is the starting value, the y-intercept. It is best taught by generating (x, y) pairs from the equation and plotting them so the straight line is DISCOVERED from a constant rate, then varying m and c independently so each parameter is bound to its visual effect. Rate contexts such as distance-time (where gradient = speed) give the numbers meaning, and the graph-as-picture and slope-height misconceptions must be confronted directly.
bestPractices: Build the line from a table of values first, so 'constant rate produces a straight line' is discovered rather than asserted.
Vary m and c independently and watch the effect: a larger m steepens the line, a negative m flips its direction, and changing c slides the whole line up or down through its intercept.
Use rate contexts (distance-time, cost-per-item) so the gradient means something real — speed, price per unit — not a bare number.
Confront graph-as-picture explicitly: a distance-time graph is a record of a relationship, not a picture of the route; a rising line is not a hill.
Contrast linear with non-linear (plot y = x^2 beside y = 2x + 1) so 'straight line' becomes a property to test, not an assumption.
keyRepresentations: Table of values → plotted points → straight line
y = mx + c with m (gradient) and c (y-intercept) annotated on the line
Distance-time graph where the gradient of the line is the speed
A family of lines pivoting (as m changes) and sliding (as c changes)
commonMisconceptions: Graph-as-picture / iconic: reads the shape of the line as a literal picture of the situation (the line goes up, so the person went up a hill).
Slope-height confusion: judges the line that is HIGHER on the graph as faster/greater, rather than the STEEPER one.
Gradient/intercept swap: reads c as the slope or m as where the line crosses the axis.
Believes every equation gives a straight line, and is surprised that y = x^2 curves.

learn.summary: A linear function y = mx + c produces a straight-line graph, where m (the gradient) is the constant rate of change — the line's steepness and direction — and c is the starting value (the y-intercept). The concept is best built by generating (x, y) pairs from the equation and plotting them so the straight line is DISCOVERED from a constant rate, then varying m and c independently so each parameter is bound to its visual effect. Rate contexts such as distance-time (gradient = speed) give the numbers meaning, and the graph-as-picture and slope-height misconceptions must be confronted directly. For ages 12-14 (KS3).

activities.title: Build the line from a table of values
feedback: If the points don't line up, check your arithmetic: each y should change by the same amount (here +2) for each step of +1 in x.
Point out that y when x = 0 is 1 — this is exactly the c value and the point where the line crosses the y-axis.
activities.rationale: Deriving the line from a value table lets 'constant rate produces a straight line' be discovered rather than asserted, and exposes the intercept concretely as the value at x = 0.
sourceClaims: KS3 pupils should 'recognise, sketch and produce graphs of linear and quadratic functions of one variable' and 'calculate and interpret gradients and intercepts of graphs of such linear equations numerically, graphically and algebraically'.
learnerActions: Take the equation y = 2x + 1 and complete a table of values for x = -2, -1, 0, 1, 2 (giving y = -3, -1, 1, 3, 5).
Plot each (x, y) pair on axes and join them.
Observe that equal steps in x give equal steps in y, and that the points fall exactly on a straight line.
State in your own words why a constant rate of change produces a straight line.
activities.intendedInsight: A straight line is a consequence of a constant rate of change, not an assumption — 'straight' is something you can test from the numbers.

activities.title: Vary m and c independently
feedback: When a learner predicts where the line will cross the axis for a given c, confirm it lands exactly at (0, c).
If a learner thinks a negative m just makes a 'smaller' uphill line, show two points and compute the change: y decreases as x increases, so the line falls.
Emphasise that changing c never changes the steepness, and that changing m never moves the y-axis crossing (it stays at (0, c)) — this separation is the key reading.
activities.rationale: Binding each parameter to its own visual role (pivot for m, slide for c) is the central conceptual payload and directly counters the gradient/intercept swap. Live sliders with a recomputing line and a synced value table can make this relationship felt; predicting the intercept before it appears tests understanding.
learnerActions: Keep c fixed and change m: try m = 1, then m = 3, then m = -2, replotting or predicting each line.

Describe what happens as positive m gets larger (the line steepens) and as m goes negative (the line flips from climbing to falling, pivoting about the same intercept); steepness depends on the size of m ignoring its sign, so m = -2 is steeper than m = 1.
Now keep m fixed and change c: try c = 0, then c = 2, then c = -3.
Describe what happens (the whole line slides up or down and crosses the y-axis exactly at c), and predict the crossing point before plotting.
activities.intendedInsight: m controls steepness AND direction (sign), while c slides the whole line to its y-intercept — each parameter is bound to a distinct visual effect.

activities.title: Distance-time race: steepness is speed, not height
feedback: If a learner picks Maggie because her line is higher at 4 seconds, take two points on each line and compute distance-per-second together, then show Emma's steeper line draws level at 5 seconds and pulls ahead afterward — steepness, not height, is speed.

If a learner talks about hills, going uphill, or the shape of a 'track', ask: 'If someone walked in a circle around their home, what would a distance-time graph look like?' Contrast a picture of the route with a record of distance over time.
If a learner names the head-start number (the 10) as the speed, change c only (steepness untouched) and then m only (line pivots), and re-read the equation to re-attach 'speed' to the gradient.
activities.rationale: A distance-time context gives gradient real meaning (speed) and directly confronts the slope-height and graph-as-picture misconceptions in one experience, especially when two lines cross so the higher-but-slower line is visible. Choosing a comparison time before the crossing (here t = 4, where the higher-at-4-seconds runner is the slower one) forces the discrimination, and the meeting point at t = 5 makes the catch-up concrete.
sourceClaims: Students confuse 'higher on the graph' with 'faster', assuming a runner is fastest because at 5 seconds her line is above another's, and make y-intercept and slope-direction errors when producing a linear graph (e.g. drawing a positive slope where negative is needed, or an incorrect intercept such as f=30); some assume two matched graphs must share the same vertical intercept.

Students interpret distance-time graphs as pictures of the situation ('as the graph goes up and down, Tom's path is going up and down'; a straight line means a straight path; a negative slope means a detour) — the graph-as-picture / iconic misconception — and misread slope direction as speeding up/slowing down; the hill-shaped graph is a deliberate distractor (Card 2 matched to interpretation E).
learnerActions: Plot two runners' distance over time on the same axes, e.g. Emma d = 6t and Maggie d = 4t + 10.
Before computing, predict who is faster and write your reason.
At 4 seconds, note that Maggie's line is higher (26 m versus Emma's 24 m), but Emma's line is steeper.
Take two points on each line and compute distance-per-second (Emma gains 6 per second; Maggie gains 4 per second).
Identify where/whether the lines cross — here they meet at 5 seconds (both at 30 m), after which Emma pulls ahead — and say what that crossing means in the race.
In the equations, identify which number is the speed (the coefficient of t, the gradient) and which is the head start (the constant, the intercept).
activities.intendedInsight: Speed is the gradient (steepness), not the height of the line; a runner can start ahead (large c) yet be slower (small m). Emma is faster because her line is steeper, covering more distance each second, even though Maggie's line sits higher at 4 seconds — until the lines meet at 5 seconds, after which Emma pulls ahead.

activities.title: Predict-then-test: does every equation give a straight line?
feedback: If a learner predicts 'straight' because 'it's an equation with x in it, like the straight ones', the emerging parabola confronts this directly — revisit the value table and show the changing step size.
Point out the symmetry of the parabola about x = 0 and that the differences between successive y-values are themselves changing, unlike the constant difference in a linear table.
activities.rationale: A prediction stated before observing is diagnostic of the all-equations-are-linear misconception, and contrasting a curve with a line beside it makes 'straight' a testable property. Contrasting the differing step sizes grounds the distinction numerically (the constant-difference test holds for equally spaced x-values, as used in the suggested tables).
sourceClaims: KS3 pupils should 'recognise, sketch and produce graphs of linear and quadratic functions of one variable' and 'calculate and interpret gradients and intercepts of graphs of such linear equations numerically, graphically and algebraically'.
learnerActions: Before plotting, predict: will y = x^2 give a straight line or a curve? Write your answer AND your reason first.
Build a table of values for x = -2, -1, 0, 1, 2 (giving y = 4, 1, 0, 1, 4), plot the points, and join them.
Plot y = 2x + 1 on the same axes for comparison.
Compare how y changes: for y = 2x + 1 the step is constant (+2 each time); for y = x^2 the steps differ (-3, -1, +1, +3), so the graph curves.
State what makes an equation produce a straight line versus a curve.
activities.intendedInsight: Not every equation is linear; a straight line requires a constant rate of change. 'Straight' is a property that depends on the equation, discovered by testing, not assumed.

activities.title: Check and consolidate: match, judge, and sort
feedback: Include a 'which line is faster/steeper' item where the correct line is NOT the one highest on the graph at the compared time, so the slope-height misconception is actively tested.
For any item answered via height rather than steepness, return to taking two points and computing the change per step.
activities.rationale: Matching, comparison, and categorisation are efficient checks of the concept; a 'higher but slower' item surfaces the slope-height misconception. These checks confirm the parameter-to-feature link rather than building it, so they work best after the dynamic exploration.
sourceClaims: Students confuse 'higher on the graph' with 'faster', assuming a runner is fastest because at 5 seconds her line is above another's, and make y-intercept and slope-direction errors when producing a linear graph (e.g. drawing a positive slope where negative is needed, or an incorrect intercept such as f=30); some assume two matched graphs must share the same vertical intercept.
learnerActions: Match each equation to its graph.
Given two straight-line graphs, decide which is steeper (and in a distance-time context, which is faster), explicitly reasoning from steepness rather than height.
Sort a set of equations into 'produces a straight line' and 'produces a curve'.
For an equation like d = 6t + 10, state which number is the gradient (speed) and which is the intercept (head start).
activities.intendedInsight: Consolidates reading gradient and intercept from both equation and graph, and distinguishing linear from non-linear, while resisting the slope-height distractor.

constraints: Matching, multiple-choice comparison, and categorisation confirm understanding but do not themselves build the dynamic link between a parameter and its visual feature; use them after exploration, not instead of it.

A static annotated y = mx + c diagram (tap m to highlight steepness, tap c to highlight the crossing point) can summarise the gradient and intercept on one line but cannot itself show the pivot-and-slide; it works as a recap card after dynamic work, not as the first teacher of the relationship.

The slope-height and graph-as-picture misconceptions must be confronted with a case where the higher line (at the compared time) is the slower one; a single rising line can reinforce rather than break 'higher = faster'.

When using Emma d = 6t and Maggie d = 4t + 10, compare at a time before the lines cross (they meet at t = 5, both 30 m); t = 4 gives Maggie higher (26) but Emma steeper and faster, with Emma pulling ahead after t = 5.

Interactive sliders, a live-redrawing line, and a synced value table are optional ways to make the equation-to-graph relationship concrete; the same insight can be reached by hand-plotting several lines and comparing them.
Require learners to state reasons, not just answers, when judging which runner is faster — the reason is what distinguishes gradient reasoning from slope-height reasoning.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The original material claimed 3D rendering 'adds nothing' and that open dialogue is not a natural vehicle; these categorical modality claims have been removed. A 3D view is not the natural representation for a two-variable linear relationship, and a coaching conversation can still probe reasoning ('how do you know Emma is faster?') — such prompts are retained inside activity feedback — without claiming dialogue cannot teach the concept.

Arithmetic checked: y = 2x + 1 over x = -2..2 gives -3,-1,1,3,5 (constant +2); y = x^2 gives 4,1,0,1,4 with non-constant differences -3,-1,+1,+3. Emma d = 6t vs Maggie d = 4t + 10 are EQUAL at t = 5 (both 30 m) and cross there, so the original row's claim that 'Maggie's line is higher at 5 seconds' is false for these numbers. The race activity's comparison has been corrected to t = 4 (Maggie 26, Emma 24), with the lines meeting at t = 5 and Emma pulling ahead afterward; the steeper = faster teaching point is preserved.

At exactly t = 5 neither runner is ahead (both 30 m); Emma leads only for t > 5, so learner-facing text describes t = 5 as the meeting/catch-up point and 'pulls ahead afterward' rather than an overtake exactly at 5 seconds.
The constant-difference argument distinguishes linear from quadratic only for equally spaced x-values; this condition is built into the suggested tables.

assess.poeTask: Before plotting anything, ask the child: 'Will y = x^2 give a straight line or a curved one? Write down your answer AND your reason first.' Then have them build a table of values for x = -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, plot the points, and join them. The reason stated before observing is the diagnostic part: children who predict 'straight' because 'it is an equation with x in it, like the straight ones' reveal the all-equations-are-linear misconception, and the emerging parabola confronts it directly.
probeDeeper: At the very start (0 seconds) Maggie's line begins higher than Emma's. Does starting further ahead mean running faster? Why or why not?
Suppose Emma's race is d = 6t and Maggie's is d = 4t + 10. Which number tells you the speed, and which tells you the head start?
If the two lines crossed at some point, what would that moment mean in the race?
Would a runner who is gradually slowing down give a straight line or a curved one — and why?
assess.correctAnswer: Emma is running faster, because speed is shown by the steepness (gradient) of the line, not by how high it is: a steeper line covers more distance in each second. Maggie's line being higher at 5 seconds only means she was further ahead at that moment, not that she is faster.

errorPatterns.pattern: Slope-height confusion: 'Maggie is faster because her line is higher up the graph at 5 seconds' — reads vertical position as speed rather than steepness
errorPatterns.nextMove: Take two points on each line and compute distance-per-second together; show that the steeper line overtakes, so steepness (not height) is speed.
errorPatterns.distractor: Maggie — at 5 seconds her line is higher up the graph, so she must be the faster runner.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Chooses Maggie and justifies by how high her line sits, not by how steep it is.

errorPatterns.pattern: Graph-as-picture / iconic: reads the line as a literal picture of the route (a rising line means the runner went uphill; a steeper line means a steeper hill)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Ask the classic MAP prompt: 'If someone walked in a circle around their home, what would the graph look like?' Contrast a picture of the route with a record of distance over time.
errorPatterns.distractor: The steeper line just means that runner's track went up a steeper hill.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Talks about hills, going up, or the shape of the track rather than distance-over-time; may pick the 'steeper hill' reading.

errorPatterns.pattern: Gradient/intercept swap: when reading an equation like d = 6t + 10, names c (the 10) as the speed or m (the 6) as the starting distance
errorPatterns.nextMove: Bind each parameter with the slider — change c only and the steepness is untouched; change m only and the line pivots — then re-read the equation.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Surfaces on the follow-up equation probe, not the runners graph: the child attaches 'speed' to the wrong number.

errorPatterns.pattern: Believes all equations give straight lines: expects y = x^2 to be straight and is surprised by the curve
errorPatterns.nextMove: Build a table for y = x^2 alongside y = 2x + 1 and plot both; the curvature is discovered, and 'straight' becomes a property that depends on the equation.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Surfaces on the POE / follow-up, not the runners graph: predicts 'straight' for y = x^2 because 'it's an equation like the others'.

responseLevels.gap: Picks the higher line as faster, or reads the graph as a literal picture of the route; makes no link between steepness and speed.
responseLevels.full: Identifies Emma as faster because gradient = speed, distinguishes head-start (intercept) from speed (gradient), maps both onto the equation, and predicts a curve for a non-constant rate — relating the parameters and transferring to a new case.
responseLevels.partial: Says the steeper line is faster, and can point to gradient and intercept when prompted, but cannot yet explain how m and c act together or map them onto the equation form (d = 6t vs d = 4t + 10) — lists the features without relating them.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here are two straight-line graphs showing two runners' distance from the start over time, drawn on the same axes. At 5 seconds, Maggie's line is higher than Emma's line, but Emma's line is steeper. Who is running faster — and how do you know?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who understands gradient-as-rate chooses Emma and justifies by steepness; a child holding the slope-height misconception chooses Maggie precisely BECAUSE her line is higher. The two reasoning paths give opposite first-tier answers, and the required reason (tier two) reveals whether 'faster' is being read from steepness or from height — a child cannot easily land the right answer for the wrong reason here.
